title: Vasudeva Datta
html:
The Singer Madhuvrata

Among Sri Chaitanya's companions there are many singers and benefactors, but of one of them Krishnadasa Kaviraja speaks in a special way: he wished to take upon himself the sins of the whole universe. This is Vasudeva Datta, the elder brother of Mukunda Datta. Krishnadasa Kaviraja calls him Vasudeva Datta, simply Vasudeva or Datta, and “the Lord's great-souled servant”; Vrindavana Dasa calls him “Vasudeva Datta Mahashaya”; Lochana Dasa, “Vasu Datta”; Kavi Karnapura, “the one jewel of the Datta family” and “Mukunda's elder brother”; the “Prema-vilasa,” “a vessel of Prabhu's mercy.” The biographies call him Sri Vasudeva Datta Thakura and Datta Thakura, and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati calls him “a servant of Vaikuntha.”1

Who he is in Krishna's eternal pastimes, Kavi Karnapura tells us:

“The two singers of Vraja, Madhukantha and Madhuvrata, are Gauranga's singers Mukunda and Vasudeva Datta.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 140)

Madhuvrata — “he whose vow is honey” — is a name for the bee: a singer of Vraja who never ceases drinking Krishna's sweetness. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta cites the same verse in his “Anubhashya” to CC, Adi 12.57, and the “Prema-vilasa” says the same: Vasudeva Datta is called Madhuvrata (22.14). In Vraja and in Gaura's pastimes alike, the two brothers are the Lord's singers.

Karnapura's poem has a verse about him too:

“Sri Vasudeva, the one jewel of the Datta family, on seeing Gauranga-chandra, at once sank wholly into the ocean of His love and for ever became as though inseparable from His very life.” (“Chaitanya-charita-mahakavya” 13.146)

That is, he became as dear to the Lord as life itself.

Family and Birthplace

Vasudeva Datta came from Chittagong (Chattagrama) in eastern Bengal, now in Bangladesh. Vrindavana Dasa writes:

“The greatest Vaishnavas, Pundarika Vidyanidhi, Chaitanya Vallabha and Vasudeva Datta, appeared in Chattagrama.” (CB, Adi 2.36)

The biographies add that he was born in the village of Chhanhara, in the area of the Patiya police station, ten kroshas (about twenty miles) from Mekhala, the village of Pundarika Vidyanidhi. The “Prema-vilasa,” however, names the brothers' ancestral home differently:2

“In the land of Chittagong there is the village of Chakrashala; there lived the respected Datta family of the Ambashthas. In that family were born two bhagavatas — Sri Mukunda Datta and Vasudeva Datta. That both brothers are devotees of Krishna, everyone knows; Vasudeva is the elder, Mukunda the younger. Both came and settled in Navadvipa — two dear servants of Sri Krishna Chaitanya Prabhu.” (“Prema-vilasa” 22.4–7)

The Ambashthas are the vaidyas, the physician community; Karnapura indeed calls Vasudeva “the best of physicians” (bhishag-rishabha, mahakavya 17.32). He was not a brahmana by birth, and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta notes this particularly when he tells how the brahmana Yadunandana Acharya honoured him as his guru — of which more below. Mukunda Datta, the Lord's companion from childhood, was his younger brother; Vasudeva himself says to the Lord, “Though he is younger, Mukunda…” (CC, Madhya 11.140).

Vasudeva was a householder: the Lord Himself says of him that he is a grihastha and must provide for his family (Madhya 15.95). In Karnapura's drama “Chaitanya-chandrodaya,” Shrikanta, listing for the Lord those who are coming to Puri, names “Vasudeva's son” among them (Act 10); one manuscript of the drama reads “Vasudeva's two children.” No one gives the son's name. Nor are the years of his life known: neither the sources nor the biographies name the year or day of his appearance or departure, and his days are not in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

In Navadvipa

Like Mukunda, Vasudeva settled in Navadvipa and became one of the foremost among Mahaprabhu's companions: he sang in the sankirtana at Srivasa's house and in the streets of the town, and the Lord delighted in his company, seeing in him every Vaishnava virtue. According to one of the biographies, at Mahaprabhu's own suggestion he was present every night at Srivasa's house when the kirtana pastimes took place; Vrindavana Dasa names a “Vasudeva” among those who took part in these kirtanas (CB, Madhya 8.112–116). Another biography adds that his voice was lovely and he knew the “Sangita-shastra,” the science of music, well.

The brothers' countryman Pundarika Vidyanidhi lived secretly in Navadvipa, in his house in Mayapur, behaving like an ordinary worldly man, and none of the Vaishnavas knew who he really was. Vrindavana Dasa writes:

“Only Mukunda and Vasudeva Datta knew the glory of Pundarika Vidyanidhi's divine love.” (CB, Madhya 7.43)

The “Prema-vilasa” says the same (22.54). One of the biographies explains that Mukunda, Vasudeva and Gadadhara were also from Chittagong and knew Pundarika.

When the Lord led Navadvipa in kirtana to the Kazi's house, Vasudeva, according to one of the biographies, was among the countless devotees of that town sankirtana; and Vrindavana Dasa names a “Vasudeva” among the singers of the procession (CB, Madhya 23.151, 23.209).

Other poets too remember him in Navadvipa. Lochana Dasa, at the opening of his “Chaitanya-mangala,” writes: “…in the feet of Vasu Datta and Mukunda is my hope” (1.28), and names him among the companions who descended with the Lord (8.623). According to Jayananda, shortly before His sannyasa the Lord called Mukunda Datta, Govinda the blacksmith, Chandrashekhara, Acharya Hari, Vasudeva Datta, Shuklambara and others to go with Him across the Ganges to Katwa (Vairagya-khanda 24.12–14); and at Lakshmipriya's feast Vasudeva is also among the guests (Nadiya-khanda 55). The late “Advaita-prakasha” says that Vasudeva Datta received mantra from Advaita Acharya.3

In Kumarahatta

Later Vasudeva moved to Kumarahatta, also called Kanchanapalli (now Halisahar), near Kanchrapara, where his closest friends Srivasa Pandita and Shivananda Sena lived. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Anubhashya” (to CC, Madhya 15.93) that Shivananda and Vasudeva lived in Kumarahatta, or Halisahar, and in Kanchrapara; one of the biographies calls him just so: “Srila Vasudeva Datta Thakura, resident of Kanchanapalli.”

The Meeting in Nilachala

After taking sannyasa the Lord went to Puri, and from there set out to wander through South India. When news of His return reached Bengal, the devotees of Gauda were overjoyed; Krishnadasa Kaviraja names Vasudeva Datta among them (Madhya 10.81). From then on he came to Puri every year with the devotees of Gauda, led by Advaita Acharya:

“Advaita, Nityananda, Mukunda, Srivasa, Vidyanidhi, Vasudeva, Murari and all His other servants came together every year and stayed four months, and with them the Lord enjoyed many kinds of pastimes.” (CC, Madhya 1.255–256)

Murari Gupta (4.1.4, 4.17.5) and Lochana Dasa (8.623) also name him among those going to Puri, and Devakinandana writes in his “Vaishnava-vandana”: “There went Vasudeva Datta Mahashaya, to whom Krishna sells Himself” (part 4, 95).

When the Gaudiyas first came to Nilachala, King Prataparudra watched them from the palace roof, and Gopinatha Acharya named each of them for him:

“This is Hari Bhatta, this is Sri Nrisimhananda; this is Vasudeva Datta, and this is Shivananda.” (CC, Madhya 11.87)

In Karnapura's drama Gopinatha tells Sarvabhauma: “This is Vasudeva, Mukunda's elder brother” (Act 8).

There too, at Kashi Mishra's house, the Lord affectionately calls by name even those He had never seen, and Gopinatha repeats His words: “Are you well, Raghava? Is all well, Vasudeva?..” (“Chaitanya-chandrodaya” 8.38).

The Lord met the devotees and had a kind word for each. For Vasudeva He had a special one:

“The Lord was delighted to see Vasudeva, and, laying His hand on him, He said: ‘Though Mukunda has been with Me since childhood, I feel greater joy in seeing you.’ Vasu said, ‘Mukunda obtained Your company; he obtained Your feet — that was his second birth. Though he is younger, Mukunda has now become my elder. He is the recipient of Your mercy, and so he excels in every quality.’” (CC, Madhya 11.137–140)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta remarks that such was Vasudeva: free of pride himself, full of respect for others. Seniority among devotees is measured not by birth but by nearness to the Lord: Mukunda had taken shelter at His feet first, and the elder brother honoured the younger as his elder. Karnapura gives the same exchange; in his drama Vasudeva replies: “The time of the Master's mercy is the time of birth; so, though he is younger, he is my elder brother.”4

And at once the Lord gave Vasudeva a service:

“The Lord spoke again: ‘I have brought two books from the South for you. Svarupa has them; copy them for yourself.’ Vasudeva was delighted to receive the books. Every one of the Vaishnavas made a copy for himself, and so, little by little, the two books spread everywhere.” (CC, Madhya 11.141–143)

These were the “Brahma-samhita” and the “Krishna-karnamrita,” which the Lord had found in the South.

The Lord's Singer in Nilachala

At the Ratha-yatra the Lord divided the devotees into seven kirtana groups. The third was led by his brother:

“He formed another group with Mukunda as the leader, in which Vasudeva, Gopinatha and Murari sang, with two more, Shrikanta and Vallabha Sena; and Haridasa Thakura danced there.” (CC, Madhya 13.40–41)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta notes that the first of the five responsive singers was Vasudeva Datta.5

In the days of Gundicha the Lord and His companions played in the waters of Lake Indradyumna, and Vasudeva was among them:

“Vidyanidhi played in the water with Svarupa, and the two, Gupta and Datta, played together.” (CC, Madhya 14.80)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains: Datta is Vasudeva Datta.

And in the Aitota garden by the Gundicha temple, he alone sang for the Lord's dance:

“The Lord danced beneath every tree, while Vasudeva Datta alone sang. Beneath each tree he sang a new song, and Gauraraya danced alone in supreme ecstasy.” (CC, Madhya 14.98–99)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains briefly: the Lord dances, Vasudeva Datta sings kirtana. Karnapura in his mahakavya paints the scene at length: in the garden the sweet Vasudeva, “the best of physicians,” sang tender songs in solitude, delighting his Beloved; whatever he sang, the Lord, hearing it from His dear one, felt it doubly, and, showing in His body all eight sattvika-bhavas — tears, trembling, hair standing on end, stupor, perspiration — He danced, no longer master of Himself.

“Thus the Lord, having created with Vasudeva a most graceful rasa of dance, and playing lightly round about, here and there, came to the bank of the pond.” (“Chaitanya-charita-mahakavya” 17.39)

The same poem of Karnapura tells of the preparations for Puri: Srivasa joyfully tells Vasudeva and Shivananda that the time of the chariot has come and a day must be fixed, and Vasudeva and Shivananda, warmly attached to each other, set out with the pilgrims (14.14, 14.25). When King Prataparudra summoned Advaita and sent a palanquin for Him, Advaita, in awe of Gauranga, took Vasudeva Datta with Him as His companion (14.58–60). In Puri Rama Pandita and Vasudeva bowed down to the Lord together (14.97), and two vessels of Ganges water — one for the bathing festival, the other for the Lord Himself — were brought by Vasudeva and Shivananda (14.101). And in Karnapura's drama the Lord says to Paramananda Puri, “Lord of the Puris! What pleases Me is just Vasudeva's conduct,” and Puri replies, “Truly he is fortunate: the Lord praises him even in his absence” (Act 10).

Sarakhela

Vasudeva's generosity knew no bounds: whatever came to him he gave away that same day, for service and for others, without a thought for himself. When, after one Ratha-yatra, the Lord was taking leave of the devotees of Gauda, He gave his friend a special charge concerning him:

“Respectfully He said to Shivananda Sena, ‘Please look after Vasudeva Datta. He is extremely generous: whatever comes to him on any day, he spends that same day and keeps nothing back. He is a householder, and a householder needs to save; without savings he cannot support his family. Let all the income and expenses of his household be in your hands. Be his sarakhela, his guardian, and manage his affairs.’” (CC, Madhya 15.93–96)

Sarakhela means a steward, a guardian of the household. This is no reproach: the Lord is caring for the home of His devotee, who saves nothing, and through him He teaches all Vaishnava householders. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes just so: this is an instruction to the Vaishnava householder about his duties in the world; and one of the biographies sees in the charge a lesson for family men — to set aside for the support of the family.

The Prayer for All Living Beings

On that same day of farewell the Lord turned to Vasudeva:

“Then the Lord embraced Vasudeva and began to describe his qualities as if He had a thousand mouths. Hearing his own qualities praised, Vasudeva Datta felt ashamed. Clasping the Lord's feet, he made a petition: ‘O Lord, You have descended to deliver the world. Please grant me one request. O merciful Lord, You are able to do anything. If You only wish it, it happens without effort. My heart breaks to see the suffering of living beings. O Lord, place the sins of all living beings on my head. Let me take the sins of the living beings and suffer in hell for them. O Lord, cure all living beings of the disease of material existence.’” (CC, Madhya 15.158–163)

It is this prayer that Krishnadasa Kaviraja recalls when he lists the branches of the Chaitanya tree:

“Vasudeva Datta was the Lord's great-souled servant; even with a thousand mouths one could not tell his virtues. He wished to take upon himself the sins of every living being in the world and suffer in hell himself, if only they could be set free.” (CC, Adi 10.41–42)6

The “Prema-vilasa” gives his petition thus: “Prabhu, grant me this boon: let all living beings go to the abode of Vaikuntha. Taking upon myself the sins of all beings, I shall suffer hell for ever for their sake” (22.10–11).

The Lord's answer is the heart of the whole account:

“When Mahaprabhu heard this, His heart melted, and with tears, trembling and a faltering voice He began to speak: ‘Such words are no wonder coming from you: you are Prahlada himself. Krishna's grace rests on you in full. Whatever His servant asks for, Krishna makes true. He has no task other than fulfilling His servant's desire. You have desired the deliverance of all beings in the universe, so all will be delivered without suffering for their sins. Krishna is not powerless; He holds all power. Why, then, would He make you suffer the fruits of sin? Anyone whose welfare you desire has become a Vaishnava, and Krishna removes all the sins of a Vaishnava.’” (CC, Madhya 15.164–169)

“You are Prahlada himself” is praise of his quality: like Prahlada, who prayed not for himself but for all who suffer, Vasudeva thinks only of the good of others (the “Anubhashya” has: “Vasudeva Datta Thakura is Prahlada himself”). The Lord goes on: Krishna will liberate the universe by his mere wish, and it is no labour for Him. Millions of universes are like fruits on a single tree: if one falls, the tree loses nothing; to the Lord of countless Vaikunthas the whole material world is like a pot of mustard seeds, and the loss of one seed goes unnoticed. In support the Lord cites the “Brahma-samhita”: Govinda awards each his karma, from the tiny insect to Indra, but burns to ashes the karma of His devotees (5.54) — and the prayer of the personified Vedas from the “Bhagavatam” (10.87.14) (CC, Madhya 15.170–180).

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta unfolds the meaning of the answer:

“Sri Krishna is all-powerful; He can free every living being from its desire for material enjoyment. You, seeing all equally, prayed on behalf of all beings, high and low, for their welfare. So by your prayer all will be delivered without suffering [the fruits of] their sins, and you will not have to suffer the fruits of sin for them in exchange. Those whose welfare you desire will become Vaishnavas, and Krishna will also save them from suffering the fruits of a Vaishnava's past misdeeds. In other words, they will give up serving sin and piety and become pure servants of Krishna.” (“Anubhashya” to CC, Madhya 15.167–169)

How the Lord fulfilled His promise Haridasa Thakura reminds Him: even a glimmer of the holy name destroys all sins (CC, Antya 3.61), and the Lord began the sankirtana, the loud chanting of Krishna's names, and so delivered all beings, moving and non-moving:

“When Vasudeva petitioned You on behalf of the jivas, You agreed to release them.” (CC, Antya 3.73)

So Vasudeva's prayer was fulfilled not by his torments but by the Lord's mercy and the power of the holy name.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta sets this prayer beside the faith of Christians in Jesus, who came to bear the sins of the world — and he does so in order to show how different and how much higher it is:

“Sri Vasudeva Datta Thakura, one of Sri Gaura's associates, like Thakura Sri Haridasa, taught the living beings of the world a universal Vaishnava love for the whole world, endless millions of times more exalted and more generous.” (“Anubhashya” to CC, Madhya 15.162–163)

In Vasudeva, he goes on, were united the giving up of worldly self-interest, the true “good of others” — service to Vishnu — and one's own true good. He saw in Gaurasundara Bhagavan Himself, and begged Him to lay on him not merely the “sins” of souls but the very disease of their existence — their aversion to Krishna, a mass of offences more terrible than any sin. Such compassion is beyond the imagination of the best karmis and jnanis of all the fourteen worlds.7

And Srila Bhaktisiddhanta adds a warning: people of the world of duality, who honour the ideals of karma and jnana, on hearing that Vasudeva wishes to suffer hell, may out of natural envy and duality praise him as a “righteous man” or rank him with a “knower of Brahman.” But his compassion is endless millions of times greater than that, and this is no exaggeration but impartial truth. By the coming of such servants of Gaura, “pained by the pain of others,” the whole earth and the whole race of living beings are blessed; in describing such a selfless maha-bhagavata the pen of poet and historian achieves its highest purpose, for the servant of Sri Krishna Chaitanya is “greater than the great and weightier than the weighty.” One of the biographies, explaining for the reader, calls him in English a “greater altruist” — “a great man who lives for others”; but his essence is not worldly philanthropy but the compassion of a servant of Vaikuntha who wants only one thing: that all souls should turn to Krishna.

“I Am Sold to Vasudeva”

In 1514–1515 the Lord went from Puri through Bengal towards Vrindavana. From Shantipura, from Advaita's house, He came to Kumarahatta, to Srivasa's house, and here His neighbours hurried to Him:

“At that moment Vasudeva Datta came, accompanied by Shivananda Sena and other devotees. Vasudeva Datta is boundlessly dear to the Lord; by the Lord's mercy all divine truths are known to him. Vasudeva Datta is the benefactor of the whole world. He is compassionate to all living beings and intoxicated with the sweetness of the love that Lord Chaitanya brought. He saw only virtues in everyone and noticed faults in no one.” (CB, Antya 5.18–21)

A maha-bhagavata, he longed for the good of everyone and loved Hari, the guru and the Vaishnavas with all his heart.8 The Lord, seeing him, embraced him and wept, and Vasudeva, falling at His feet, sobbed aloud; and such was his weeping, says Vrindavana Dasa, that even those whose hearts were hard as stone or wood could not keep back their tears; there was no one to compare with him (5.22–25).

And then the Lord said of him wonderful words:

“So great was the Lord's love for Vasudeva Datta that He said, ‘I belong to Vasudeva.’ Again and again Sri Gaurasundara said: ‘My body belongs to Vasudeva Datta. Vasudeva Datta may sell Me whenever he wishes. This is truly so and not otherwise. Krishna will always protect anyone touched by a breeze that has touched the body of Vasudeva Datta. O Vaishnavas, listen! I speak the truth! My body belongs to Vasudeva alone.’” (CB, Antya 5.26–30)

Hearing of this mercy of the Lord to Vasudeva, the Vaishnavas joyfully sang the holy names (5.31). The Lord, entirely free, the Master of all, gives Himself by His own will to the love of His pure devotee: this is His nature — He is bhakta-adhina, conquered by the love of His servants. The words “sold” and “belong” speak of no bargain and of no dependence of God on a man; they are the language of love: such was Vasudeva's love that the Lord called Himself his property.

Jayananda describes the same meeting: Shivananda Sena and Vasudeva Datta came to Srivasa's house, and the Lord spoke of Vasudeva's greatness: He called Himself “Vasudeva's purchased servant” and told Srivasa that Vasudeva Datta enables Him to reveal Himself (Vijaya-khanda 5.26–27); he also tells that at the festival in memory of Madhavendra Puri at Advaita's house, “how to serve patol, bathua and shak — this Vasudeva Datta knows” (5.18). And Vrindavana Dasa, listing those going to Puri, recalls these words again:

“Also came Vasudeva Datta, to whom Lord Krishna has sold Himself.” (CB, Antya 8.14)

The “Charitamrita” adds that on this journey the Lord Himself visited his home:

“The Lord stayed there one day, and in the morning He came to Kumarahatta, where Shrinivasa lived. From there He went on to Shivananda's house, and after that the Lord came to the house of Vasudeva.” (CC, Madhya 16.205–206)

According to Karnapura's drama, the roads to both houses had been decorated, and Vasudeva begged the Lord first to grace Shivananda's house with His presence; the Lord did so, and then looked in on Vasudeva for a moment and went back to the boat (Act 9). Even in the joy of receiving the Lord, Vasudeva thought first of his friend.9

Year after Year

In the years that followed, too, Vasudeva Datta went to Puri with the devotees of Gauda (CC, Madhya 16.16; Antya 10.9; 12.13). The devotees brought the Lord dishes cooked at home, and Govinda, His servant, as he served them, named who had sent them:

“These are from Vasudeva Datta and Murari Gupta, and these various kinds from Buddhimanta Khan.” (CC, Antya 10.121)

And those who were not brahmanas — Vasudeva Datta, Gadadhara, Murari Gupta, the people of Kulinagrama and of Khanda and others — when they invited the Lord, fed Him with prasada bought at the temple of Jagannatha (Antya 10.140–141).

When He introduced Sanatana Gosvami to His companions, the Lord presented Vasudeva Datta to him as well (Antya 4.108). And to Vallabha Bhatta the Lord said of the Vaishnavas of Bengal:

“Acharyaratna, Acharyanidhi, Gadadhara Pandita, Jagadananda, Damodara, Shankara, Vakreshvara, Kashishvara, Mukunda, Vasudeva, Murari and all the other devotees who descended in Gauda have preached the name of Krishna and prema throughout the world, and whatever devotion to Krishna I have, I have gained in their company.” (CC, Antya 7.48–50)

And Krishnadasa Kaviraja opens one of the chapters of the “Charitamrita” with the words: “Glory to Mukunda and Vasudeva, and glory to Haridasa!” (Adi 13.3).

When the Lord sent Jagadananda Pandita to Navadvipa, to mother Shachi, old friends met him in Bengal:

“Vasudeva and Murari Gupta were delighted to have Jagadananda; they kept him in their homes and would not let him go. From his lips they heard the most intimate stories of Chaitanya, and in the joy of those stories they all forgot themselves.” (CC, Antya 12.98–99)10

Yadunandana Acharya

Vasudeva Datta's mercy touched also the guru of Srila Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami. Krishnadasa
Kaviraja writes in his list of Advaita's branches:

“Sri Yadunandana Acharya is a branch of Advaita; his own branches and offshoots are past all writing. He received the mercy of Vasudeva Datta and with all his heart took shelter of Sri Chaitanya's feet.” (CC, Adi 12.56–57)

And in the account of Raghunatha's flight from home:

“He had received the favour of Vasudeva Datta; he was Raghunatha's guru and family priest. He was an intimate disciple of Advaita Acharya, and at the Acharya's order he held Chaitanya to be the treasure of his life.” (CC, Antya 6.161–162)

Karnapura in his drama calls him “the teacher Yadunandana, most sweet, the beloved of Sri Vasudeva” (“Chaitanya-chandrodaya,” 10.3), and one of the biographies, “the vessel of Vasudeva Datta Thakura's boundless mercy.” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta makes it precise: Yadunandana is “dear to Vasudeva Datta Thakura, that is, an object of his mercy, but not his disciple”; he received initiation from Advaita. And at the same time: “Vasudeva Datta Thakura was not born in a brahmana family by seminal descent, yet Yadunandana regarded him as his own guru, who had bestowed mercy on him.” So a brahmana honoured a Vaishnava of the vaidya community as his guru and benefactor, for a Vaishnava is not defined by birth. The “Charitamrita” calls Raghunatha Dasa Yadunandana's disciple and Yadunandana his guru; but here too, explaining Karnapura's words “his disciple is Raghunatha,” Srila Bhaktisiddhanta makes it precise: “that is, an object of his mercy — not that he received initiation from him in particular.”11

Madana-Gopala in Mamgachi

In Modadrumadvipa of Navadvipa, on the Howrah–Katwa railway, a mile from the Purvasthali stop, lies the village of Mamgachi, the birthplace of Thakura Vrindavana Dasa, son of Narayani, Srivasa's niece. Here Vasudeva Datta installed the Deity of Sri Madana-Gopala. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta wrote in the “Anubhashya”:

“In the village of Mamagachi, the birthplace of Thakura Vrindavana, the Sri Madana-Gopala he established still resides. His service is very much neglected. It is desirable that His service be made splendid.” (“Anubhashya” to CC, Adi 10.41)

According to one of the biographies, Madana-Gopala stood in a dilapidated temple. According to another, Madana-Gopala is now served in the temple of Saranga Thakura in Mamgachi, before a bakula tree, beside Radha-Gopinatha, and pilgrims on the Navadvipa parikrama come here for darshana. In the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math, on the day of the Modadrumadvipa parikrama, “the places of appearance of Srila Vrindavana Dasa Thakura and of the Deities of Sri Saranga Murari and Vasudeva Datta Thakura” are named.12

Vasudeva's care for Vrindavana Dasa is also bound up with Mamgachi. The “Prema-vilasa” relates that while Vrindavana was still in the womb his father Vaikunthadasa left this world, and Srivasa took the widowed Narayani into his home; as a child of five Vrindavana settled with his mother in Mamgachi, and

“Vasudeva Datta, a vessel of Prabhu's mercy, maintained Vrindavana together with his mother. They lived at Vasudeva Datta's temple, and Vrindavana began to study the various shastras.” (“Prema-vilasa” 23.71–72)

One of the biographies writes that Narayani, widowed, lived in poverty at Vasudeva Datta's house, serving there, and that Vrindavana Dasa was born there.13 Narayani is an eternal associate of the Lord, who received His remnants as a child; her life at Vasudeva's house and temple was her service and his care for her, not a worldly humiliation. So the future author of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” grew up and studied beside Vasudeva Datta's Deity.

Remembrance

Lochana Dasa, in a chapter found only in one edition of his poem, names Vasu Datta among the devotees who cried out when the Lord entered Jagannatha at Gunjabadi.14

The padas remember him too. In Vasu Ghosha's song of how Gauranga left Nadiya, “Vasudeva Datta, Murari and Vakreshvara weep” with all the devotees of Navadvipa. And in Vishvanatha Chakravarti's anthology “Kshanada-gita-chintamani” one pada — on Gaura, the “king of dancers” in Navadvipa — bears his name: “…Vasudeva Datta is enraptured”; in the “Padakalpataru” the same pada is signed by Govinda Dasa, so whether Vasudeva composed padas remains uncertain.

Vaishnavas glorify him in the “Vaishnava-vandanas”: “I glorify Vasudeva Datta, full of greatness: by the touch of the breeze from his body people at once attain prema” (part 1, 42; cf. CB, Antya 5.29); “…Vasudeva Datta, whom the Lord kept with Himself in Utkala” (part 2, 26); “from the breeze from his body prema-bhakti for Krishna is born” (part 5, 29). In the “Narottama-vilasa” Narottama in a vision beholds him among Gaura's dancing companions (7.117). When Vasudeva Datta left this world, the sources do not say.

Narahari Chakravarti entreats him as well in the “Namamrita-samudra,” a collection of appeals to the Lord's associates — together with Uddharana:

“Vasudeva Datta, Uddharana, Purandara! Save me — so cries this wretched sinner.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 24)

His Significance

Vasudeva Datta's life teaches the boundless nature of a Vaishnava's selfless love: he sought nothing for himself — neither wealth, nor liberation, nor even escape from hell — and desired only that all souls should turn to Krishna. The Lord called Himself his property and promised that anyone whose good Vasudeva desired would become a Vaishnava. Haridasa Thakura linked his prayer with the Lord's sankirtana, which delivered the moving and the non-moving; Srila Bhaktisiddhanta placed his compassion above all ideals of righteousness and knowledge.15 To his brother he yielded seniority, to his friend the honour of receiving the Lord first; and Mahaprabhu's words “This body of Mine belongs to Vasudeva” remain an eternal witness to how the Lord yields to the love of His servant.

  1. He should not be confused with his namesakes: Vasudeva Ghosha, the kirtana singer, brother of Govinda and Madhava Ghosha; Vasudeva Vipra, the leper brahmana of Kurma-kshetra whom the Lord healed; Vasudeva Sarvabhauma and other Vasudevas. In the lists of the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” and the “Charitamrita” where simply “Vasudeva” appears (for instance, the kirtanas at Srivasa's house or the procession to the Kazi), the source does not always make clear who is meant.

The brothers were of one family, so there is no real contradiction; but which village, Chhanhara or Chakrashala, was their home remains unclear.

But according to Vrindavana Dasa and the “Prema-vilasa,” Vasudeva lived in Navadvipa and was with the Lord even before His sannyasa (CB, Madhya 7.43), and the “Charitamrita” does not speak of a first meeting in Puri.
